Factors such as fluctuating market prices, advancements in technology, and location- specific conditions can significantly impact both capital expenditures and input costs. Consequently, any future plant’s actual capital and input costs may differ substantially from the assumptions within the TEA, potentially altering the overall costs and economic viability of the HC production facility. Therefore, the TEA outputs are best utilized as a comparative tool, enabling a direct comparison between different HC production pathways and evaluating the economic potential of different feedstock options. The technology pathways modeled within the TEA were carefully selected and tailored to the specific characteristics and processing requirements of each feedstock type, ensuring a comprehensive and insightful assessment of the various HC production routes. The study’s primary goal is to identify the most promising and cost-effective pathways for HC production within the targeted region, considering the available resources and economic factors. 30 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3 New England Jet A and SAF Logistics 3.1 General SAF and Jet A Logistic Considerations The method of moving fuels throughout the country depends on the location of production, fuel type, and volume. The modes of fuel transport include barge, tanker (ship), pipeline, rail, and truck (Figure 21). Each mode operates under regulations and standards that protect quality and safety. Pipelines carry multiple fuels, barges can transport several fuel types with multiple tanks, and the same railcar type is used for biofuels and petroleum products, but they are generally leased and used for a single product over the period of that lease. Where pipelines are not available, dedicated trucks are used to move Jet A from terminals or refineries to airports where pipelines are not available.9 There is also the consideration of how and where to blend SAF and Jet A. Previous studies identified terminals as the optimal location for blending due to existing tanks, associated equipment, blending software, trained staff, insurance, and permits covering these activities. Today, nearly all SAF is blended with Jet A at terminals (Moriarty, Milbrandt, and Tao 2021).10 Section 3.2 evaluates New England considerations on receipt, storage, and blending of SAF and Jet A. SAF produced at a stand-alone plant meets ASTM D7566 and is delivered to terminals tanks for certification testing. SAF is then blended with Jet A into a third tank, tested, and certified as ASTM D1655. The blended fuel is then delivered to airports by the same trucks and pipelines used today (Figure 22). Another potential production and fuel receipt method would be if a petroleum refinery coprocessed SAF. In this instance, SAF would be coprocessed alongside Jet A, certified as ASTM D1655 at the refinery, and delivered through the supply chain as Jet A is today. 9 Airports that do not have pipelines receive fuel by truck.
